details: IAEA waste classification (IAEA GSG-1 2009; updated 2022): VLLW (Very Low Level Waste): <100 Bq/g; bulk disposal in controlled landfill; contaminated soil; building debris; LLW (Low Level Waste): 100 Bq/g to ~1 MBq/g; near-surface disposal; institutional waste; ion exchange resins; short-lived; ILW (Intermediate Level Waste): ~1 MBq/g to 10 GBq/g; requires shielding during handling; solidified in cement or bitumen; intermediate repository; structural materials; HLW (High Level Waste): >10 GBq/g; significant heat generation; requires deep geological disposal; primary: spent nuclear fuel; vitrified reprocessing waste; ILW-LL: intermediate level long-lived waste (significant quantities of alpha emitters; t½ > 30yr; depth disposal required); pre-2009: some countries used: LILW-SL (short-lived) / LILW-LL (long-lived) / HLW; US: Class A/B/C/GTCC (Greater Than Class C); Russian: class 1/2/3; EU directive 2011/70/Euratom: common framework
chernobyl_application: Chernobyl waste categories: (1) NSC material: corium/FCM (HLW + HLW-LL; ~170-220t); graphite fragments (ILW-LL; C-14 t½=5730yr; Nb-94 t½=20,300yr); (2) CEZ contaminated soil: VLLW to LLW depending on location; (3) Spent fuel (ISF-1 + ISF-2): HLW; (4) Decommissioning debris (Units 1-3): LLW to ILW; (5) Red Forest buried material: LLW to ILW (surface burial trenches = inappropriate for ILW; groundwater pathway problem); (6) Contaminated vehicles ('Elephant graveyard'): LLW to ILW; total CEZ waste volume estimate: 2.5-3.0 million m³ contaminated material (most VLLW/LLW); ~800 official waste sites in CEZ

details: CEZ waste site inventory (2026): Total registered radioactive waste sites: ~800 (DAZV/SNRIU registry); Total waste volume: 2.5-3.0 million m³ (Ukrainian government estimate; includes: contaminated soil removed during decontamination 1986-1990; debris from sarcophagus construction; contaminated equipment; vehicles; felled Red Forest trees (buried in trenches); fire hoses; personal protective equipment; biological materials; NSC: contains corium/FCM/fuel particles/structural debris (not counted in surface burial inventory; covered by NSC); major waste site types: shallow trench burial ('могільники'; hastily constructed 1986-1987); temporary waste stores (ventilated containers); ISF-1/ISF-2 (permanent engineered facilities for spent fuel); SRWT (Solid Radioactive Waste Treatment facility; operating 2015+); burial trenches: ~145 sites within 10km of NPP; significant contamination of shallow groundwater (Sr-90 3-4 orders above WHO at some sites)
chernobyl_application: Waste retrieval challenge: most 1986-1987 burial trenches not properly engineered (no liner; no cover); location coordinates partially uncertain (some documented only by rough hand-drawn maps; chaos of 1986 prevented systematic documentation); systematic survey: IAEA-funded GPR (ground-penetrating radar) survey 2010-2015 located ~90% of known trenches; re-survey after 2022 war: incomplete; Red Forest trenches: primary groundwater contamination source; Sr-90 leaching from buried tree debris (fuel particles dissolving; half-time 5-25yr); solution: selective excavation + proper containment vs in-situ stabilization (polymer injection); EBRD Shelter Fund includes provision for waste management ($90M allocation for near-site waste)

details: Spent nuclear fuel (SNF) classification: legally: most countries classify SNF as HLW pending reprocessing decision; Russia: reprocesses VVER fuel (resource); Ukraine: RBMK and VVER SNF = treated as waste (no domestic reprocessing capacity); RBMK fuel characteristics at discharge: burnup: 20,000-35,700 MWd/tHM; fissile content: U-235 ~1.1% remaining; Pu-239 ~0.8%; Pu-240 ~0.3%; Pu-241 ~0.1%; heat generation: ANS-5.1 decay heat at t=25yr post-discharge: ~39 W/assembly (see chernobyl_spent_fuel_isf2_REAL.csv); specific activity at discharge: ~10¹⁵ Bq/tHM; at 25yr: ~10¹³ Bq/tHM; dominant nuclides at 25yr: Cs-137/Ba-137m; Sr-90/Y-90; Am-241 (growing from Pu-241); Pu-239 (very slow decay); Cs-137 dominates gamma field; Sr-90 dominates beta; Am-241 growing alpha hazard
chernobyl_application: ISF-2 classification under Ukrainian law: 'Wet' or 'Dry' spent fuel storage are NOT final disposal; legal status: interim storage pending final repository; Ukraine does not have deep geological repository; target: Chestiv dry cask final repository (site selected; design phase 2020+; operational target 2045+); RBMK fuel NOT reprocessable as-is (unique fuel bundle geometry; zircaloy rather than standard zircaloy-4); comparison: VVER fuel sent to Russia for reprocessing pre-2022; post-2022: Ukraine processing shift to domestic storage; Onkalo Finland (operational 2025) = world's first operational deep geological repository (VVER fuel); no RBMK-specific DGR exists globally

details: Corium/Fuel Containing Materials (FCM): HLW category; 170-220 tonnes inside NSC; composition: UO₂ fuel melted with Zr cladding + steel + concrete → lava-like FCM (= 'Elephant's Foot' material and dispersed throughout lower reactor levels); physical state: solid glass-ceramic; primary phases: SiO₂-Al₂O₃-ZrO₂-UO₂ glass matrix (COGEMA studies); U content: ~15-20% by mass; radioactive inventory (April 2026): dominated by Cs-137 (Ba-137m), Sr-90, Am-241, Pu-239/240/241; neutron flux: Room 305/2 has fissile material (U-235 + Pu-239) in corium; neutron multiplication factor k_eff monitored by NFC sensors; stable since 2022; NO plan to remove corium (technology does not exist; dose rates unmanageable); current strategy: 'safe confinement' = let NSC protect for 100yr; waste classification implications: FCM = HLW requiring deep geological disposal eventually; timeline: beyond 2200 when NSC reaches end of design life
chernobyl_application: NSC design life: 100 years (2116); at end of NSC design life: FCM still highly radioactive; Cs-137 will be 3.3 half-lives decayed (12.5% remains); Sr-90: 3.3 half-lives (12.5%); Am-241: beyond its 2058.7 peak (declining but still significant); Pu-239: effectively unchanged (3.3×10⁴yr t½); long-term waste challenge: corium cannot be left indefinitely in degrading structure; POST-NSC plan: hypothetical options: (1) second confinement structure; (2) robotic dismantlement + waste packaging (technology unavailable 2026); (3) in-situ grouting + second barrier; current Ukrainian position: NSC is solution for this generation; next generation must plan for post-2116

details: RBMK reactor graphite waste: 1700 tonnes nuclear graphite (pre-accident inventory); fate: ~100-150 tonnes ejected/dispersed (fuel particles + graphite fragments); ~10-15% burned during fire (170-250t); remaining: ~1300t in-situ (mixed with corium/debris; within NSC); graphite long-lived radionuclides: C-14 (t½=5730yr): produced by N-14(n,p)C-14 from nitrogen impurities in graphite; estimated C-14 in RBMK graphite: ~25 TBq total inventory (N-14 concentration ~100 ppm in nuclear graphite); C-14 concern: mobile under oxidizing conditions (CO₂ form); slow release over thousands of years; Nb-94 (t½=20,300yr): Nb-93(n,γ)Nb-94; present in structural steel adjacent to reactor and graphite; essentially permanent on human timescales; fraction in graphite: ~0.1 TBq total from all activated materials; very low but ultra-long-lived = deep geological disposal argument
chernobyl_application: Graphite waste global context: UK has ~100,000 tonnes graphite from Magnox/AGR reactors (primary graphite waste challenge in UK nuclear decommissioning); IAEA EPRI joint study: graphite waste should be classified as ILW-LL (not VLLW) due to C-14 mobility; Chernobyl graphite: in-situ (cannot be removed from corium mass); will remain in NSC indefinitely; C-14 from Chernobyl graphite = ~25 TBq; long-term: C-14 biological uptake if CO₂ form (plant photosynthesis); dose calculation: 25 TBq × 10⁻⁶ Sv/Bq effective dose coefficient for C-14 inhalation × release fraction (very small) = negligible pathway for foreseeable future; Nb-94 is gamma emitter (702 keV; 99.85%) = long-term repository heat/radiation concern

details: Radioactive waste treatment technologies applicable to Chernobyl: (1) Cementation: ILW solidification; contaminated liquids + Portland cement → stable matrix; volume: 1 m³ liquid → 1-2 m³ cementite; leach rate: ~10⁻⁶-10⁻⁷ g/(cm²·day) for Cs-137; standard for: ion exchange resins; evaporator concentrates; contaminated oils; (2) Bituminization: ILW/LLW; liquid concentrates + bitumen (asphalt); lower volume factor (1:1); concern: combustible; limited use post-Chernobyl; (3) Vitrification: HLW → borosilicate glass; leach rate 10⁻⁹-10⁻¹⁰ g/(cm²·day); used for reprocessing HLW (COGEMA La Hague; Sellafield BNFL; Mayak Russia); not currently used for Chernobyl FCM; (4) Compaction: LLW metal waste; volume reduction 5-10×; SRWT at ChNPP: commissioned 2015; processes: cementation of LLW; compaction of metallic waste; incineration of combustibles; plasma torch processing
chernobyl_application: Current Chernobyl waste management (2026): SRWT annual capacity: ~3,000 m³ waste/year; materials processed: contaminated PPE from decommissioning work; ion exchange resins from water treatment; tools; filter media; backlog: estimated 100,000+ m³ legacy waste requiring processing; key challenge: Category ILW-LL waste (long-lived; requires interim storage pending DGR); Ukraine's Vektor complex (within CEZ): designed as near-surface repository for LLW; construction 1994-2022; some capacity used; war: construction delayed; Phase 2 (ILW cells): on hold; SNRIU regulatory review ongoing; waste characterization: HPGe analysis of all containers before acceptance (radionuclide identification); minimum criteria: no HLW accepted at Vektor

details: Contaminated soil as waste: Volume above regulatory limits requiring action: Cs-137 > 37 kBq/m² = 125,000 km² (UNSCEAR 2008; 3 countries); top 5 cm of soil (primary activity layer): volume = 125,000 km² × 0.05m = 6,250 km³ = 6.25 × 10⁹ m³; mass: 6.25 × 10⁹ × 1500 kg/m³ = 9.4 × 10¹² kg = 9.4 billion tonnes; CLEARLY IMPOSSIBLE to excavate; actual remediation approach: (1) Only immediate vicinity (CEZ): soil removed from roads; playgrounds; schools during 1986-1990 decontamination; (2) Agricultural countermeasures (not removal): K-fertilizer; liming; plowing; (3) Restricted land use for highest areas; (4) In-situ: leave contamination; manage exposure via behavior/food restrictions; ICRP 111 (2009): protective actions for contaminated areas; NOT based on removing soil; criteria for when soil removal justified: public dose reduction > 1 mSv/yr annually
chernobyl_application: Soil self-decontamination: natural processes reducing external gamma dose: radioactive decay (Cs-137 t½=30.17yr); soil migration (Cs-137 fixed by FES clay; 90% in top 5cm after 40yr; BUT this migration reduces DOSE RATE: as Cs-137 migrates from surface into soil, gamma self-shielding increases → effective source shielding by 3-5 cm of soil provides ~50-70% reduction beyond pure radioactive decay); weathering/erosion: lateral redistribution; vegetation cycling: minor; net effect: dose rate in Pripyat declining ~3-5%/yr vs 2.3%/yr pure radioactive decay = significant natural remediation contribution; NO large-scale excavation justified or feasible outside CEZ

details: Global nuclear waste context (2026): Spent nuclear fuel: ~440,000 tonnes heavy metal (tHM) accumulated globally; annual generation: ~12,000 tHM/yr; Chernobyl Unit 4 inventory: ~192 tHM (reactor fuel at time of accident); CEZ total SNF (ISF-2): 21,217 assemblies × ~185 kg = ~3,930 tHM; HLW from reprocessing: ~200,000 m³ globally (in temporary storage at La Hague; Sellafield; Mayak; Savannah River; Hanford); Hanford: 177 underground tanks; 56 million gallons waste; primary US legacy waste; deep geological repositories operational: Onkalo (Finland; VVER; operational 2025); under construction/planned: Sweden Forsmark; France Bure; Belgium; Germany (Konrad for ILW; Gorleben controversy resolved 2022 → Standortauswahl); US Yucca Mountain: politically stalled since 2010; Chernobyl uniqueness: only nuclear accident where HLW (FCM) is in-situ in the accident site
chernobyl_application: Policy context: No deep geological repository exists that could accept Chernobyl FCM; corium composition (SiO₂-Al₂O₃-ZrO₂-UO₂ glass-ceramic) chemically similar to nuclear waste glass (designed to be stable for 10,000yr); irony: Chernobyl accident produced a 'self-vitrified' nuclear waste glass in-situ; this glass has been extensively studied (Pazukhin; Borovoi; IAEA studies); stability: Room 305/2 water contact → Cs-137 leaching documented (primary pathway for groundwater contamination); but leach rate of dry FCM: ~10⁻⁸ to 10⁻⁷ g/(cm²·day) (similar to borosilicate glass); conclusion: NSC keeping FCM dry = primary waste management action; NSC water removal system essential
